content.title: The Kalman Filter as Recursive Bayesian Estimation, With Numbers
content.text:
A Kalman filter is Bayesian updating with Gaussians and a linear model, plus the observation that every step produces another Gaussian, so you only ever track a mean and a covariance. The block-matrix formulas are bookkeeping for that one fact.

Set up the model. The hidden state at step k is x_k. It evolves as x_k = F x_{k-1} + w_k, where w_k is zero-mean Gaussian noise with covariance Q. You observe z_k = H x_k + v_k, where v_k is zero-mean Gaussian with covariance R. You start with a belief that x_0 is Gaussian with mean m_0 and covariance P_0. The filter alternates two steps.

Predict: push the belief through the dynamics. The predicted mean is m_k^- = F m_{k-1} and the predicted covariance is P_k^- = F P_{k-1} F^T + Q. The minus superscript means before seeing z_k. Uncertainty grows here.

Update: condition on the measurement. Compute the innovation y = z_k - H m_k^-, the innovation covariance S = H P_k^- H^T + R, and the gain K = P_k^- H^T S^(-1). Then m_k = m_k^- + K y and P_k = (I - K H) P_k^-. Uncertainty shrinks here.

The gain looks arbitrary until you derive it in one dimension, where H and F are both 1. You have a prior on x that is Gaussian with mean a and variance p, and a measurement z with variance r. Multiplying the two Gaussian densities gives another Gaussian whose precision (inverse variance) is the sum of the precisions, 1/p + 1/r, and whose mean is the precision-weighted average of a and z: (a/p + z/r) / (1/p + 1/r). Multiply top and bottom by p r and rearrange: mean = a + (p / (p + r)) (z - a). So K = p / (p + r), the prior variance divided by the total variance. Large p pushes K toward 1 and you take the measurement; large r pushes K toward 0 and you keep the prior. The posterior variance is p r / (p + r) = (1 - K) p, matching the update formula. The matrix version is the same computation with inverses standing in for reciprocals.

Now numbers. One-dimensional random walk, F = 1, H = 1, Q = 1, R = 2. Start with m_0 = 10 and P_0 = 4.

Step 1. Predict: m^- = 10, P^- = 4 + 1 = 5. Measurement z = 12. Gain K = 5 / (5 + 2) = 0.714. Update: m = 10 + 0.714 * (12 - 10) = 11.43. P = (1 - 0.714) * 5 = 1.43.

Step 2. Predict: m^- = 11.43, P^- = 1.43 + 1 = 2.43. Measurement z = 11. K = 2.43 / 4.43 = 0.548. m = 11.43 + 0.548 * (11 - 11.43) = 11.19. P = 0.452 * 2.43 = 1.10.

Step 3. Predict: m^- = 11.19, P^- = 2.10. Measurement z = 13. K = 2.10 / 4.10 = 0.512. m = 11.19 + 0.512 * (13 - 11.19) = 12.12. P = 0.488 * 2.10 = 1.02.

The gain and covariance are converging to fixed values, and neither depends on the measurements. For any time-invariant linear Gaussian model, K and P follow a deterministic recursion and can be precomputed. The steady state satisfies P^- = (P^- R / (P^- + R)) + Q. With Q = 1 and R = 2 this becomes (P^- - 1)(P^- + 2) = 2 P^-, or (P^-)^2 - P^- - 2 = 0, so P^- = 2, K = 2 / 4 = 0.5, and the posterior variance P = 1. Our example is within 3 percent of that after three steps. In steady state this filter is an exponential moving average with weight one half: a Kalman filter on a random walk is an EMA whose decay factor is set by the ratio Q/R rather than hand-tuned.

So Q is less a description of physical noise than a knob controlling how fast the filter forgets, and here a non-obvious asymmetry appears. Suppose you set Q too small, 0.01 instead of 1, believing the state barely moves. Solve the steady state again: (P^-)^2 - 0.01 P^- - 0.02 = 0 gives P^- of about 0.146 and K of about 0.068. If the true state jumps by 5, the first update corrects only 0.34 of it, and the remaining error decays by 0.932 per step: about 10 steps to halve, 33 to reach 90 percent correction. Meanwhile the filter's own P is 0.136, so it reports a standard deviation of 0.37 while actually off by 4.7. Worse, any downstream logic that gates innovations by claimed variance, as most real systems do to reject outliers, will reject the true signal and never recover.

Now set Q too large, say 10. Steady-state P^- is about 11.6 and K about 0.85, so the estimate jitters with roughly 85 percent of the measurement noise. But its error is bounded by that noise, it tracks jumps within a step or two, and its reported covariance is honest. Under-confidence costs variance you can see; over-confidence costs bias you cannot, unbounded and self-reinforcing. When you must guess Q, guess high, then check the normalized innovation squared over a run: it should average about the dimension of z, and if it runs well above that, Q needs to go up.

notes: Dense math exposition: predict/update equations, gain derived as a precision-weighted average, a 3-step 1-D worked example that converges to clean steady-state numbers, and an asymmetry argument about process-noise misspecification. A correct judge should rate it high-value and note that the over-confidence conclusion (error unbounded vs bounded by R) is specific, not a platitude.
